utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, the Prosecution and the Defence and the accused. I apologise for being late. It is not because of my colleague, but it is my own fault. For various reasons I was delayed this morning. Let us resume, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We have a new witness, Tomislav Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He's not a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, no protection measures have been envisaged. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, sir? It is the President who is speaking to you. Can you hear me? Tell us your name, your age, your occupation, your residence and then you will make the solemn declaration. We're listening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Tomislav Rajic. I was born on the 25th of May, 1959 in Travnik. I am a graduate of the School of Law. I am currently living as a refugee in Vitez municipality, Guca Gora 1B, Travnik municipality. That is my current address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please make the solemn declaration according to the text given to you by the usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. You have agreed to come and testify at the request of the Defence in the trial against General Blaskic, the accused who is here present. You will first be answering questions by the Defence, then the Prosecution, and then the Judges will probably have some questions for you. Mr. Nobilo, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rajic. You have already introduced yourself, but could you tell us, before the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and before the conflict, what were you doing? What was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: After the first democratic and free elections held in December 1990, on the 22nd of February, 1991 I was appointed the municipal secretary for National Defence. I held that post until the 31st of December, 1993, after which I became chief of staff of the Travnik HVO brigade, and I held that position until the 20th of May, 1994, when I transferred to the municipality again where I worked in the department for administration and social services, and after the 27th of November, '96 I was appointed head of the municipal authorities of Travnik based in Nova Bila, which is the Croatian part of the authorities of Travnik. After the elections in 1997 for joint authorities, I was appointed president of the municipal council of Travnik, and I held this position until the 24th of November this year, when I resigned because I was not satisfied with the work of the joint bodies of government in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this testimony we will focus on that period of your life when you were secretary of the municipal secretariat for National Defence of Travnik municipality. That is, the period of '92 and '93. That is what we're going to focus on. Before we discuss your functions, could you tell us, after the first free elections how was the civilian government in Travnik organised? Tell us the structure of the civilian authorities, and were those authorities formed jointly by the Serbs, Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: The communal structure was such -- or, rather, the municipal structure was such that local elections were held for the municipal assembly. The municipal assembly had a total of 60 deputies representing all three nations living in Travnik. The president of the municipal assembly was the highest representative of the municipal authorities, he had his secretary, and the executive of the municipal authorities was the executive board of the municipal assembly. In every municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were these executive bodies, including Travnik. Again, this executive body had its department, such as the department for the economy and finance, or, rather, it was called a secretariat in those days. Then there was a secretariat for general administrative affairs and social services. Then there was a municipal secretariat for National Defence, then a municipal secretariat for internal affairs, that is the police, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we were to compare this with the state -- with a state, could we say that the executive board of the municipal assembly of the town could be compared with what is, at the state level, described as the government?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that was the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, the -- what are ministries at the state level, at the municipal level were known as secretariats?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only department that we'll be discussing is the department or secretariat for National Defence. Was this a civilian body or was it a military body?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: These were exclusively civilians but it had some responsibility over military structures. For example, when the JNA made a call-up for regular military service, then upon the request of those military bodies the department would operate, even though all the officials were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Our immediate superior was the president of the executive board of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was head of the civilian executive body. Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: His superior was the president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the municipal bodies you have said that there was a secretariat for National Defence. Can you describe to us the internal structure of this secretariat, of which you were the head, and could you tell us what individual departments within the National Defence secretariat actually did?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: The National Defence secretariat had three entities. At the head of each of those entities was a person in charge. One of those was the military department, the second was the department for Civil Defence, and the third was the centre for observation and information as it was called then. As for the competencies of each of these services, the military department kept complete records of men capable of military service, that is, conscripts. They kept records of men as soon as they reached the age of 17. When their ability to do military service would be checked, that would be done when he becomes 18. Then he would be sent to actually do his military service in the year when he becomes 19. This was the rule. So this department was in charge of this military service. Then, also, they kept records of people who had completed their regular military service but were in the reserve of the former JNA and the Territorial Defence. Then there were personnel files of military officers in reserve, then of the reserve policemen. Then there was a courier service, a messenger service, which was organised in such a way that they would personally deliver call-out papers to conscripts. Then, also, there were records regarding the enlistment to civilian bodies in state of war or immediate threat of war, people would have the work obligation to work in a particular enterprise under those conditions. These were the responsibilities of the military department. The Civil Defence department did not envisage any active service in the Civil Defence, but there were two basic components. There were units, Civil Defence units, general purpose Civil Defence units. These were units that -- from which work platoons would be manned. Then there were special purpose units for first-aid, for the removal of ruins and for other such needs, which also determined the occupational structure of the people belonging to these units, whereas the third part of the National Defence secretariat was the centre for observation and information. It was a service which would be operative around the clock, and any negative occurrences or any incidents that may occur in the municipality would be reported to them. They also had to monitor the air space, as far as that was possible. This centre actually collected information that was forwarded to me, and then I would forward it on to the President of the executive board or the president of the municipality in case of any extraordinary circumstances or any emergency that may have occurred within the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The structure of the authorities, as you have described them, functioned roughly until the summer of 1992 when a division occurred. Before that, the assembly, as the basic body, stopped operating. Can you tell us how the authorities split, how it was divided and what were the criteria?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: You see, at the end of 1991 certain problems cropped up in the work of these joint bodies of authorities and the secretariats I refer to, and these bodies were composed in accordance with the election results. That is, the number of votes won by each of the three national parties. The Serbs were the first to walk out of the joint bodies. They simply withdrew, and the elected bodies ceased to function. In formal terms, the same bodies remained in power until roughly the summer of 1992, at least as far as my secretariat is concerned. We continued working in the same offices in which we had worked until then, but each individual was working in favour of members of his own people, if I can put it that way. The Bosniak Muslims formed their own presidency, which took over the competencies of the assembly, so that we had two parallel bodies with the same powers. The only thing being that one was manned by people of one ethnic group and the other by people of the other ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now refer to the Croatian faction of the civilian authorities. You said that you remained in the same premises but each one was servicing his own people, to put it that way. In the structure of the secretariat of National Defence that we are particularly interested in, which now came to be called the defence department, were there any changes in the organisational structure and in its practice and the implementation of regulations?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Regarding the changes that occurred, the first were informal and personnel terms. The services and departments remained more or less the same, only the names changed. What was called the secretariat was now called the department for the economy and finance, the department for defence and so on. Then also there were changes in personnel. We had split along ethnic lines, though we did co-exist together still.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the organisation remained the same. Before I proceed to my next questions, could we, with the help of the usher, distribute an act of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? We have copies for the interpreters to make their task easier, and we're glad to say that we have a French copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm very happy to hear that, Mr. Nobilo. You must have made our translators work day and night to have it ready for you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D492, 492A for the French version, 492B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The first is in Croatian. The first is the Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on to the text itself, tell us: In the former State, there were federal and republican laws; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And both laws were valid throughout the territory of the country, that is, for the federal laws, and the republican ones were applicable only to the republic to which they applied; but in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both the Yugoslav laws and the republic laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in force. Will you please look at this decree, and I will read a part of Article 1. In Article 1, the second sentence says: "Work obligation units shall be organised by assigning to them citizens subject to work obligation and not assigned to the armed forces or subject to work obligation in bodies of the Interior Ministry." Could you explain this for us? What was the principled position taken?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In the former Yugoslavia, all of us had a task in the case of war or the immediate threat of war. All those who were not assigned to JNA units - in the reserve forces, in the Territorial Defence, in the Civil Defence units, or in the Interior Ministry - were subject to work obligation. They could have had this obligation within their own enterprises, which, according to plans, were to continue to function in case of war or threat of war, and some enterprises were declared to be of special interest in case of war, and therefore, all people working in those enterprises and who held essential functions in such an enterprise, they were assigned to those duties or their work obligation would be executed in their own enterprises. The rest, those who were not employed in such enterprises, were subject to work obligation in other places; for instance, to load and unload things, to secure certain premises, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can it be said then that it was a constitutional category that all citizens are duty-bound to contribute to the defence of the country in two forms: either by military service or work service, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, it was the right and duty of each and every citizen to participate in the defence of the country. Through these various forms that I have mentioned, each one of us had a specific assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody was not in the army, he was subject to work obligation?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. The work obligation was the last in this hierarchy because the priority was to man the JNA and the reserve units, then the Civil Defence and Territorial Defence, and then those who were left over would be subject to this work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the remainder, those were not engaged, right? So now let us move on to Article 3 of this former Yugoslav decree where units are established. Work obligation units. They are squads, battalions, even brigades. These are military terms, but does this mean that they grow into a military unit, or is this still a civilian structure except that they had military names, these groups of civilians had military names?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: These were exclusively civilians, and they could be attached to military units but the names remained as such, so that one would know how many men were needed; for example, if you would say "platoon," if you would say "company," we would know exactly how many men were involved. For example, if I needed 15 men or if I needed 70 men, I knew what I was talking about, so it is military terminology but the members were civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to read Article 4, and I believe that it is highly relevant to this debate, and then I am going to put a question to you. "Article 4. Work obligation units for the needs of the armed forces in war shall be organised in peacetime by order of the competent municipal body issued on the basis of a request of the competent military-territorial authority. "In war, if pressing needs of the armed forces for the conduct of combat operations and other needs so require, and the competent municipal body is in no position to issue an order to the effect of paragraph 1 of this Article, work obligation units shall be organised by order of the officer in charge of the competent military territorial authority, or by order of a military officer holding the post of commander or an equivalent or superior position (hereinafter: the commanding officer)." So could you please interpret this for us? As a rule, who establishes work obligation units, as a rule?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: As a rule, it was the executive council of the Municipal Assembly in normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a civilian authority of government; right? And when does the military directly establish units, work obligation units? When?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: When these civilian authorities of government do not function, then, at the request of the military officer in charge, a certain work obligation unit can be established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us digress in terms of this specific example. To the best of your knowledge, in Vitez and Busovaca, in '93, and in '92 also but primarily in 1993, were the civilian authorities in the municipality actually operating?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 6. I would like to read out a few parts which I believe to be relevant. Article 6 reads as follows: "In discharging tasks and jobs for the needs of the armed forces, work obligation units may be assigned to the following tasks: "(1) work on fortification ..." And then, line 4 from the end of this paragraph, not to read all of it, says that they can be engaged to dig dugouts as well as carrying out "other work in the directions and in the areas and zones of combat which ensure the more successful execution of the missions of units of the armed forces." So my question to you is: In keeping with this Article, could a work obligation unit be engaged for fortification works where combat action is taking place?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, but in addition to that, there is this last point, 7, which always leaves the possibility of using them for other purposes in terms of the needs of the armed forces. That is what our legal regulations were like. It directly did stipulate what was supposed to be done, but other things that could not have been envisaged because not all specific situations can be envisaged in a legal enactment. So it was quite natural for these units to be engaged in the zone of combat as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us look at it from a logical point of view. After all, fortification, as a rule, is in combat zones.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, as a rule, and this can also be done in-depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, as a reserve position.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, as a reserve position. But this was the frontline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 7, procedures referred to, and I shall read it out because I believe this is important, so it reads as follows: "The commanding officer in charge shall submit a request to the competent municipal body stating all the elements needed for the organisation of work obligation units (the number and strength of the work obligation units; the structure and organisation of each unit; for whose needs they are being organised; the area and time at which the mission will be carried out; the manner and place of the reception by military units; the equipment, tools and machines the unit must have, etc.)." And Article 8: "On the basis of the request of the commanding officer in charge, the competent municipal body shall organise work obligation units, assign persons subject to work obligation to their duties, assign material, supplies and animals in accordance with the regulations on the material obligation of citizens and basic and other organisations of associated labour," et cetera, et cetera. So can we say that this regulates who asks for a work obligation unit and who establishes it? Do we have this kind of division of duties between the military and civilian authorities? What do the military authorities ask for and who establishes a work obligation unit? Who selects the people who are going to be on this unit? Is it a civilian authority that does this?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, it was as follows: When there is a need, then the commanding officer in charge asks the Department of Defence in the municipality for a certain number of people in order to carry out certain tasks. Since the Department of Defence has records of all military-age men and are capable of military duty and military service and they also have a call-up service, and this call-up service can get in touch with the persons concerned, then it is this municipal body that calls up a specific person in order to man a work obligation unit if a squad is required or a platoon or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us simplify matters. Can we say that the military authority gives a certain request, "We need 30 people in 24 hours," and then the civilian authority carries out this selection and chooses the people who are going to be on this unit and sends this unit?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say that it depends on the civilian authorities whether it is one man or another man who is going to dig trenches, for example?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, the civilian authority reaches a specific person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another question now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D493, D493A for the French version, D493B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, document 493 that we have in front of us, is this a republican piece of legislation from the domain of National Defence, and is this a law, rather, a decree, issued by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, this a republican decree regulating work obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Article 2, the last point, it says that the tasks and jobs that are mentioned in Article 1 shall also include "outfitting and building of shelters, fortifications," et cetera, "and other works of special importance to all-people's defence." Let us be quite specific: By definition, "fortification works," are they trenches, communication trenches, et cetera, so in terms of the former JNA terminology and the Secretariat of National Defence? Was that so?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, trenches, communication trenches, roads, et cetera, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 4 says that: "Work duty details shall be replenished with the necessary material," et cetera, and "Persons subject to work duty and have no other war duty station shall be assigned to work duty details." Does that mean what you said, that those who do not have any other duties are assigned to work obligation units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Articles 5 and 6, look at them. Let us not quote all of them. Are they quite clear in terms of the competence of the civilian authorities for establishing work obligation units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, and I have already spoken about that, I think. Every one of them had a working plan, every municipality had a plan of work and a plan for wartime and these units were involved, but, as I said, after the war broke out, these plans fell apart, the ones that we had elaborated together, I mean, the members of all the ethnic groups that lived together in that territory. So then everyone made out his own plans. But we still had the same regulations and we all worked according to the same methodology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also like to read out Article 9: "The municipal secretariat for national defence shall be in charge of the enlistment of, maintenance of records on and notification of their scheduled stations to persons assigned to work duty details and the calling up of members of those details when it is ordered that they be recruited to carry out the jobs and tasks from Article 2 of this Decree." Is that the regulation that you spoke of, that the municipal department of National Defence, a civilian authority, mobilises people for assignment to work units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could we have the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D494, D494A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No French version now, Mr. Nobilo. Obviously the translators were exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One should not expect too much from translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may for one moment, counsel. Mr. President, in Prosecutor's Exhibit 38, I do believe there is a French version of this. So that might help the Court. I'm almost positive there is a "Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." This is, I believe, the first document about to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it a Prosecution Exhibit, number 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. These are the series of documents that were used during the testimony of Professor Pajic, in the examination conducted by Mr. Cayley. And if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Dubuisson, I believe it's tab 2 in that document. That is the degree on armed forces; is it not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. Please continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention just to three relevant Articles. I believe they are relevant. They're brief, and I'm going to read them to you and then I'm going to put a question. This is just above Article 3, and the title reads: "Defence Duties of Citizens." "Every citizen of the HZ H-B shall have the duty to protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the HZ H-B, and in particular; 1. Serve in the army. 2. Perform compulsory work service the army. 3. Participate in Civil Defence. 4. Participate in monitoring and reporting service. 5. Be subject to requisitioning requirements. Citizens shall be assigned duties under items, 1, 2 and 3 of this article in accordance with defence plans and requirements." Now, point 1. Compulsory Work Service, Article 4: "All able-bodied citizens over the age of 16 who have not been assigned to the armed forces shall be subject to compulsory work service. Compulsory work service shall be introduced in the HZ H-B in the event of war or the immediate threat of war, and shall be formed in compliance with the administrative plans and orders of the HVO." Article 5: "Compulsory work service shall not apply to: - persons serving in the armed forces, - women over the age of 55, - pregnant women, - men over the age of 65." Mr. Rajic, tell us, basically was the work obligation basically regulated in the same way in these regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as it was in Bosnia and Herzegovina and previously Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. It was practically rewritten except for terminology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get some more detailed bylaws or other specific laws that would regulate the work obligation from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or was this the only document you had?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This was the only document we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this situation what did you draw on? What was the prevailing practice in your work, because obviously this is a basic document, and it does not regulate this area in sufficient detail.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: We who had worked in defence departments had sufficient experience. We know how this was done, on the basis of the regulations that were relevant in the former Social Republic of Bosniz-Herzegovina, in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, to the best of your recollection, the community of Herceg-Bosna, did it suspend in any one of its decrees the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have thus concluded the examination-in-chief. Documents D493, 494 and 492, we offer them into evidence. But I see here in the transcript that the interpreters could not hear your answer, witness, so I asked you whether you knew that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna suspended in any one of its decrees, the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so could you please reply into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I do not know of any suspensions of any regulations of the Social Republic of Bosniz-Herzegovina, because we continued to work according to these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We have thus concluded our examination-in-chief and we would like to offer into evidence these three exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection, especially as one of the exhibits was already submitted as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Rajic, it is the turn of the Office of the Prosecutor to ask you questions. So it's Mr. Kehoe. The witness is yours. Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Rajic, and to a fellow lawyer, welcome to the Tribunal. I would like to introduce you to both myself, my name is Greg Kehoe, I work in the Office of the Prosecutor. My colleagues, to my immediate right is Mr. Harmon, Mr. Mark Harmon, and to his right is Mr. Andrew Cayley. So we welcome you. As a lawyer, Mr. Rajic, I would like to ask you a few questions. If we could start just briefly on the Exhibit D492, which is the SFRY document that you discussed just briefly. Did you have that in front of you, sir? If not, if I can ask the usher to provide it. Now, Mr. Rajic, just looking at that document, that is a document that appears was published in the official gazette of the SFRY on the 8th of July of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. We've been talking about 1993 so much in this trial I need to drop ten years. 1983. Excuse me. Now, tell me about this, Mr. Rajic. This particular document was a document passed by the then former Yugoslavia, and it was binding on all of the republics; is that correct? And the republics we're talking about are Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, Vojvodina and Kosovo depending how you term that, but it was binding on all those entities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, it is, for the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was a body of representatives for all of those republics that were in existence in 1983; wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. It was the republican assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they vote on this?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously from what we know from the law, this vote setting up this type of organisation for the discharge of work obligations was passed by the republics and came into law on the 8th of July, 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This is not a law, it is a decree. The law was adopted earlier on total National Defence, and on the basis of this the decree is a sub-legal act, and the law on total National Defence led to this decree regulating the method of organisation and ways in which work obligations were put into practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction, Mr. Rajic, but essentially we are talking about the passage of a document in a democratic fashion, where people had the opportunity to talk and debate and discuss the relative benefits of this law before they decided to enact the law and then the concomitant decree that we see before us in Defence Exhibit 492. Would you agree with that, as an attorney, that that's how it happened?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: At that time that was how these decrees were enacted, and I agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to -- and I should have given this to you at the same time as Defence 492, but if we could have Defence 493 given to the witness. Do you have that, Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This is the republican decree of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in truly democratic fashion, the decree that we saw in Defence Exhibit 492 moved from a Federal level and then it was enacted on a Republic level, and the document that we see before us is the Republic level in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I believe that is published in the official gazette of the Social Republic of Bosniz-Herzegovina on 10 December, 1985; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, this was done in a democratic fashion, was it not, before this particular decree was enacted?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. There was the procedure in the organs and bodies which enact the decree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted to us that in December of 1990, several years after both of these decrees, was the first free elections.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we get to that, before we get to the elections, I missed a point. I just want to go back to these two documents. In both of these decrees that you have talked to us about, did you read them before you came in here today?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: That was my work, so I had to read them because, as I say, from 1991 onwards, until the end of 1993, I was the head of the -- a department, whose duty it was to know the rules and regulations under its competency and that of its secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume also that as a lawyer, and as a good lawyer, you were conscious of the provisions of the Geneva Convention as it applied to the use of civilians in labour; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also know that the Socialist Republic of the former Yugoslavia, or the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia was a signatory to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at those particular documents, and I'm talking about 492 and 493, and I know you have 493. If you want to take a look at 492 again, I invite to you ask the usher for it if you need it. In any of these decrees does it authorise the JNA, or the defence department, or the defence administration or anybody of that character to use civilians and to force civilians to dig trenches or fortifications, as you discussed with Mr. Nobilo, to force civilians to dig trenches at dangerous frontline positions? Is there anything in those laws that authorises that? Because I'm sure you know that that is illegal under the Geneva Convention, Mr. Rajic, as an attorney and has reviewed those conventions.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: They were not civilians, they were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina whose distribution work duty was this type of duty. And according to our regulations, which were relevant at that time in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, this was legal and based on the law, that is, to engage people who were to perform certain duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, in response to the questions by Mr. Nobilo, didn't you tell these Judges that those individuals on these work details were civilians? Didn't you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, we were all civilians in the State in which there were no professional soldiers, but in the case of war and the immediate threat and danger of war, we had the constitutional right and duty to participate in the country's defence, and each one of us, each one of those civilians, every peasant, farmer, worker, white collar worker had his wartime duty to perform. All those who were not engaged in performing other duties came under this particular work duty. So the work duties here enumerated -- are enumerated here, the kind of duties that were meant. So it was the legal use. Whether it was an honest use, we could discuss that point, but it was legal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, my question here is going to be very simple: Did you or did you not tell Mr. Nobilo, maybe 45 minutes ago, that the individuals that were called upon to work in these work details were civilians? Didn't you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered. The record speaks for itself asked and answered counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can I state my objection, please, without interruption? Thank you. The question has been asked and answered, and it is also improper as to form because the record speaks for itself. What he said on direct-examination is in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He should not be questioning about, "Well, on page 4, paragraph, line." If he wants to, he should show it to him. It's not a memory quiz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, calm down, Mr. Hayman. Mr. Kehoe, please rephrase your question, and I ask the witness to answer it clearly. Please put your question clearly and let the witness answer it clearly. Short question -- it's a short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a very short question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the direct testimony, in response to questions by Mr. Nobilo, did you or did you the not say that the individuals on these work details were civilians? Didn't you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Look at the Judges, please, Mr. Rajic. You're answering the question for the benefit of the Judges. So what is your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: My answer is that all those who were not involved in the military units were civilians who were engaged in other defence duties, and that was their work duty, Civil Defence observation and information and their material duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go on to your next question, Mr. Kehoe, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Geneva Conventions prohibit the use of civilians at dangerous frontline positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can't -- now they want to ask a question before they --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You did not allow Professor Degan to speak about the Geneva Conventions, and it is difficult for us to accept that our witness and colleague, who probably does have a certain amount of knowledge on this, be asked that question either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness held an official position at -- an administrative political position, but I think the question can be asked, because -- and please don't interrupt, otherwise, I will pick up those same questions. So, please answer if you know. If you don't know, you can simply say you don't know. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's also outside of the scope in the sense that as the witness is testifying as to what foreign law was as a matter of fact, as Judge Shahabuddeen pointed out in our earlier discourse. This question is not, "What was in the laws," this question was, "Well, tell us, this law appears to say this, the Geneva Conventions say such and such, interpret it for us." That is exactly the distinction that the Court drew earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know very well that it is a complex distinction. Mr. Hayman, this is not the first time I'm saying it. It is a distinction that emanates from our texts, and as I have said on a number of occasions, it is a highly subtle distinction. Secondly, we, the Judges, abide by our texts, and we are -- our ultimate aim is to establish the truth. We have a witness who can give us his view regarding the possibility of using civilians in relation to the Geneva Conventions. If it is not a question put by the Prosecution, it is a question put by the Judges. So please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: First of all, I focused on the regulations of former Yugoslavia in my work, and I don't think I can comment on the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question was whether you wondered at any point whether it was possible to make people dig trenches, and whether you ever thought that this may be outside the scope of the law. We're not asking you to make a lecture on the Geneva Conventions. I repeat it, in my own name: In implementing these texts, did you ask yourself, when sending people to dig trenches, whether respecting this text to the letter, whether it was possible or not to do that. So it is Judge Jorda asking you this question now, and please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I thought that it was legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please put your next question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a lawyer, Mr. Rajic, you would agree with me that domestic law does not override the Geneva Conventions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Outside of the scope and the kind of expert legal testimony we were not allowed to elicit from our earlier witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, go on to another question. I did repeat that previous question myself, but, please, put your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back to the free elections in reference to the two documents, the two Defence documents that we had, Defence Exhibit 492 and Defence Exhibit 493. The free elections, the free democratic elections, took place in the former Yugoslavia in December of 1990; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was December, but at the end of 1990, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other democratic elections throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina after these free elections at the latter part of 1990?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: There were no other elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just chat with you a little bit, if I could, about the next exhibit, and I know the one that you were dealing with was Exhibit 494. I think it was the Croatian armed forces, decree on armed forces. If I could give that to Mr. Rajic? Again, Mr. President, this is the -- for the French purposes, this is the 38C, tab 2, French version, but I'll just deal with the Defence Exhibit because it's a little easier at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. This allows me to follow the proceedings more easily. Go on with your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, do you have that before you, that document?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, this particular document was passed by the Croatian community in Herceg-Bosna I believe on 3 July 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims vote on it?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know. If anyone was a member of the HVO, and there were Muslims in the HVO, and if they attended the assembly of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, they probably voted. But I wasn't there, so I can't say. But I know that there were some Muslims who were in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you agree that the representatives at this time, there was a legitimate government for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was established after the free elections in 1990 that sat in Sarajevo; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: In 1992, at this time, in my opinion, there was no legitimate government because some had walked out, the others had split up, and only a few members remained representing the other nations in that government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: So that the impression may have been that it was legitimate, but that was not the government that was elected at the first free democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Rajic, this particular document, this particular law, was the law that you discussed with Mr. Nobilo and was the law that was used to set up work units and to force Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches or to build fortifications or to do other work; isn't that right? Isn't this the law that you used?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No. You are saying that. That is not what I said. The decree came into force in the middle of '92. We had work squads even before that. These work units were not formed exclusively of Muslims by the Croats and vice versa. All citizens from a certain area who were not assigned to any other wartime duty were members of these work units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you is a Defence Exhibit, Defence Exhibit 493 -- excuse me, Defence Exhibit 494, I believe, that was used in evidence, and wasn't this used to establish the legal authorisation for you to set up these work units? Wasn't that the purpose of putting this exhibit in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Objection as to the purpose of Defence counsel in offering an exhibit. That is our business, it's not the business of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me change my question, Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the legal authority that you used through 1992 and 1993 and thereafter to set up these work units? What law did you base your decision on?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: The work units had existed before, they were formed before this decree on the armed forces was passed, because the conflict, the conflict had already started, but the subsequent need for certain duties required new units to be formed in different places and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The new units that were formed after this law was passed in 1992, was this the law that was used -- the one that was discussed during your direct examination by Mr. Nobilo -- was this the law, the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was that the law that you and other members of the HVO used to order that work units be set up using Bosnian Muslims, Romany, other Croats, et cetera? Is this the law? If this is not the law, what law did you use?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This decree did not regulate in detail the method of formation or use of these units, but the other decrees, the republic decree and the federal decree, those were the ones that we used and on the basis of which we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take a look at what Mr. Nobilo read during the course of his direct examination, and look at Article 3 of that document, 494. Article 3 -- correct me if I'm wrong if I'm reading this incorrectly : "Every citizen of the (Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna) shall have the duty to protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the (Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna)" and therefore the obligation to -- at number 2 -- "perform compulsory work service." Now, is that in part what Mr. Nobilo read during the course of your direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This was copied from the law on All Peoples Defence of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that provision of the law, the law, Mr. Rajic, that you used to set up these work units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: We acted in accordance with the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but in concrete terms, we based our work on the decrees that more specifically dealt with the work obligation because this is a Decree on the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna, which is far broader, covering the rights and duties of citizens in wartime, whereas the decree on the organisation and deployment of work obligation units were based on the regulations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the federal decree which was valid for the whole territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is "Yes," this is the jurisdictional underpinning for your actions; correct?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This was a part of the jurisdiction for our activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what else was there? What other law that came into effect was there that allowed you to force Muslims into work units?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the questions, an allegation has been repeatedly made which the witness has never supported. My learned friend keeps asking, "What decrees did you use to force Muslims to dig?" This witness didn't force a single Muslim to dig. He was working in Travnik. And if he forced anyone, he forced Croats; and the Muslim authorities also forced Muslims. So why is an attempt being made to impute to the witness something that he hasn't said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am going to delete your last observation, Mr. Nobilo, because it is the right of the Prosecutor to pursue along these lines, but it is true that the first question has been repeated several times. I have another question to ask you, a more practical one: Have you got many questions, because perhaps we could take a break now, or do you intend to complete your cross-examination before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have quite a bit, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then. So we are going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can continue with our proceedings in an atmosphere of calm and tranquillity. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Always, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Mr. Rajic. We spend a lot of time together, all of us, and we laugh about things from time to time. Mr. Usher, excuse me, before you sit down, could I have 494 back with the witness, or does he still have it before him? Okay. Now, Mr. Rajic, take a look again at Exhibit 494, the document that you read with Mr. Nobilo. Let's look at Article 3 of that document. Can you take a look at that?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I can't follow if you just give me the number. Could you just tell me which document you are referring to? I have three here, but I don't know their numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What I am talking about is the Narodni List, the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're talking of the document of Herceg-Bosna, aren't you, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, it is number 494, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, let's look at the provision that you read with Mr. Nobilo, specifically Article 3. Could you read that first sentence from Article 3 for us?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: "Every citizen of the (Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna) shall have the duty to protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the HZ H-B and in particular: 1. serve in the army; 2. work service; 3. to participate in the Civil Defence; 4. the obligation to participate in the monitoring and reporting services; 5. be subject to material or requisitioning requirements."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That says, in that first sentence, that the citizens have to "protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the (Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna)." Now, the community of Herceg-Bosna, was it ever internationally recognised as a country?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not recognised as a State.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to this particular Statute, this particular decree on the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, were the authorities in Sarajevo consulted before it was enacted?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was the ultimate conclusion of the legitimate government in -- or the government in Sarajevo? What was their conclusion about the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know that the government you mention took any specific position regarding this decree of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. I think that it did not comment on this decree at all, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, where did you get your law degree, sir? In what university? Was it in Sarajevo University or some other locale?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Sarajevo University, but in Zenica. There was a department in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir. And you're aware of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you not?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges about the Constitutional Court in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Kehoe -- I am thinking of the previous objections -- you can't ask the witness to go beyond his competencies. You can ask him what he thinks about Article 3, about the independence of the territory, what independence and so on, that is fine; but to ask him what the Constitutional Court of Bosnia did and what it has to do with this, perhaps you are asking him more than he can contribute to this judicial debate. Therefore, rephrase your question, staying within the scope of this decree of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and using your guidance, I will go straight to the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you, Mr. Rajic, part of Exhibit 38, and that would be tab 22. There is a French copy of this, Mr. President, which is in 38B, tab 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can't believe it. I see the French version on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Wonders never cease, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think you should address yourself to the English language booth. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, this is a decision by the Constitutional Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 18 September 1992, and in that decision -- we will go straight to the point concerning this piece of legislation -- is that the document that is before you? Is that the decision of the Constitutional Court, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't think so. It is a decree in French having to do with the adoption of the decree with the force of law regarding nationality of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have a little problem there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you tell us out? Do you have the decree before you from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 18 September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. This is document 38, tab 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, which text do you want to show the witness? Let us be clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am trying to show him a text of this decision of the Constitutional Court of 18 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is in the Official Gazette dated 18th of September, '92, and it has to do -- it carries the number 38B/23. Is the Defence able to keep up with the debate, with the discussion now? Has the witness got the right document?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I have the Official Gazette number 16/92, dated 18 September, '92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. Yes, that's fine now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, there was a decision rendered, and take a look at the decision rendered by the Constitutional Court, and the following items were annulled, and turn your attention to number 5 which reads: "The Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which is adopted on 3 July 1992 by the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, you agree with me that based on this decision, the Constitutional Court in Sarajevo annulled that decree that was passed by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: First of all, I see this document for the first time. Secondly, in that period, there was no possible communication, or communication was not possible between Sarajevo and Travnik, where I was, so that not just I but none of us were able to have any such documents in our hands because Sarajevo was totally besieged and there were no connections with the central bodies of Bosnia, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're mindful of the fact, are you not, Mr. Rajic, that this particular decision was passed on 18 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No, I was not mindful of that fact because I didn't have time to read it, to see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with the first point on that decision, what was also annulled by this decision was the decision on the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna adopted on the 18th of November, 1991, by democratically elected representatives of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that was also annulled. Do you see that, point 1?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't see it. I'm not able to discuss with any authority something that I'm seeing for the first time, and I don't exactly know what you're referring to, Articles 1, 2, 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you a question. After 18 September, 1993, based on the decree of the armed forces of the Croatia community of Herceg-Bosna, you issued, and other members of the HVO issued orders to set up work platoons consisting of Muslims, Croats, Serbs and, I suppose, Romany well. We've heard some testimony about Romanies being called to dig trenches. And this is after the 18th of September, 1992. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No. On the basis of the decree on the armed forces of HZ H-B, I didn't order any one Muslim to be a member of a work platoon, as we Croats in Travnik were limited to a small area of Travnik municipality, and the work platoons in the area of responsibility that I covered at the time consisted exclusively of Croats and one or two Serbs who happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how about in Vitez municipality? Were orders issued to compel Muslims to join these work units in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know that orders were issued to compel Muslims to work in Vitez, because I was working in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you hear about that, Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I didn't hear about anyone being coerced, in the sense of being physically forced, but the actual idea of a mobilisation could be termed a coercive measure to engage individuals in any one of these four forms of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that conceptually you could see Muslims living in the Lasva Valley area being compelled to dig trenches pursuant to this decree on the armed forces that we've been discussing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Probably some Muslims in Vitez did dig trenches, but I know that on one occasion 13 or 18 members of a work unit who were Croats were killed in the territory of Vitez. In the majority they were Croats, and there may have been two or three Serbs who were killed on that occasion as members of a work platoon in Vitez. I did not hear that any single Muslim member of a work platoon was killed, or a Romany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the work broke out in 1993 and people were being forced to dig trenches, were representatives of the ICRC, the International Red Cross, complaining to authorities within the HVO about compelling Bosnian Muslim to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I'm not aware of those complaints, but no one complained to me, even though I did have contacts with members of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if they complained to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does your answer also include no knowledge of complaints by either ECMM or the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such complaints. As I said, I was working in Travnik, and I did have contacts with the European Monitors, and I still do. We complained to them that Travnik Croats were engaged to dig trenches in Travnik and not just to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You complained to the international authorities that you compelled Bosnia Croats to dig trenches for the HVO? Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No. You've made a different interpretation, which is something that I didn't say. I said that we had complained because -- through the European Monitors we communicated with parts of our families who were left behind in Travnik, and we knew that Croats were engaged by members of the BH army to dig trenches, and they did dig trenches but this was an obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Maybe that was a problem in the translation, Mr. Rajic, but I think I understand what you're saying. So you complained to the ECMM because you believe that the Muslim authorities were forcing Bosnian Croats to dig trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: We didn't think, I knew that they were doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you complained, Mr. Rajic, because you knew that that was illegal and wrong; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No, it wasn't illegal, it was based on the law. Whether it was ethical, that's something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you complain? If it was legal and there was nothing -- no problem under the law, why did you complain to ECMM about Bosnian Croats being forced to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Simply we were trying to protect those individuals. And given conditions, that was a privileged position in relation to other citizens in a territory covered either by the BH army or by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But essentially you complained to ECMM even though you maintain that the use of civilians, Bosnian Croat civilians to dig trenches by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an legal act; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. Although I knew it was legal, we tried to protect them somehow. They would dig trenches at HVO frontlines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, you were setting up in the Defence department -- by the way, are you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular structure, if a work order went out to compel a Bosnian Muslim to dig trenches for the HVO, what happened to a Muslim if they refused?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: In the part where I was there were no such cases, and if I were to engage in guesswork it would only be guesswork.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the statute that we talked about just previously, the one that is Defence Exhibit 494. There are, in fact, penalties that are imposed for failure to comply with a work order, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, there are some provisions relating to penalties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And part of those penalties contemplate imprisonment; isn't that right? Look at Article 59 and 60. Am I correct in that reading of the law, that if a Bosnian Muslim refused to comply with an order of the HVO to go to the frontline and dig trenches, he could be fined or he could be thrown in prison for every time he refused to answer the call? Isn't that right? If I'm not right, please tell us what this law says.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: You're not right when you are talking about a Bosnian Muslim digging for a Bosnian Croat. Reference is made to individuals here. An individual has certain responsibilities, and there are five in case of war or immediate threat of war, and all individuals were subject to this responsibility if they were on a certain territory that was under anybody's control, the HVO, the BH army. This was the responsibility of an individual, not according to ethnic background. So the individual as a citizen of that municipality and of that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, if a Bosnian Muslim in Vitez refused to go and work on the frontlines digging trenches in a work platoon after receiving an order from the HVO pursuant to Article 3 of the decree, if he refused he could be fined and he could be sent to prison for every time he refused to dig trenches for the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Theoretically that possibility did exist. However, no one had any money in those days, so these fines could not be imposed, and also, there was no place to put them up in. Regardless of ethnic background, people wanted to be in work platoons and they preferred doing that, so no one could persecute them because they were sitting at home and doing nothing while others were waging war. On the other hand, participation in a work platoon or in a work obligation was, at any rate, better for every individual than going to prison. Therefore, there were no such persons who refused to assume their work obligations and who were, therefore, detained. There were some who were detained because they refused to take part in the armed formations. I do not know of any case that someone was punished for this or -- or detained or kept in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rajic, putting a Bosnian Muslim in context, or putting you as a Bosnian Muslim sitting in Vitez, receiving an order from the HVO to work on the frontlines in a work platoon had what's known as a Hobson's choice, he either had prison or he worked on the frontline digging trenches. Those were his choices; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I've been repeating the same question -- I mean, rather, this question has been repeated for the past 15 minutes. The witness has said that the law prescribed this but it was not applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe. I the think the witness has answered. Let's go forward a little more quickly, so please move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Rajic, do you know any Bosnian Muslims that refused to go dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were talking with -- in direct-examination, with my learned friend Mr. Nobilo, that the position of the commanders was to put a request in for work platoons to work; is that correct? Did I understand your testimony in response to Mr. Nobilo's questions properly?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did Blaskic use this procedure?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of Mr. Blaskic resorting to this procedure. I had direct contact with the commander of the brigade of the municipality of Travnik, and I, as head of the defence department in the municipality of Travnik, never received any direct orders in this sense from Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive those from his immediate subordinate, the commander of the respective brigades?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: There were such requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when that request came in, Mr. Rajic, did the HVO military, either the commander or the brigade commander, in your case, did they designate the spots that these work platoons were supposed to go dig defensive fortifications?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: They decided on this in keeping with their needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the HVO military would decide what their needs were, where they needed to dig trenches in the frontline or else where, and then they would put a request in from you to send them 50 -- you know, 20, 50 or a hundred people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. First, once a work platoon is formed it is formed. It is not reformed every time a request is submitted. One knows who the members of a work platoon are, so when necessary, they go. Also, a person would be appointed who would be commander of the work platoon, and he would know where his men were at a given point in time, and then he was supposed to notify them and to call them up. So a work platoon is established once and then it is used when necessary. If the need arises for an additional number of people, then we who kept the records on all persons who were involved, then we would have a look and see whether there was a sufficient number of people and whether this request could be met or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to summarise this entire procedure, you were operating in concert and together with the wishes of the HVO military; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. We were their service for these needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, did everybody in the Lasva Valley, both in Travnik and municipality, did everybody know that these work units with civilians were digging trenches and fortifications on the frontline? Was that a well-known fact?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Everybody knew about that, that this trench digging was going on, regardless of ethnic background and regardless of who controlled which part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on what you just told us, Mr. Rajic, do you assume that Colonel Blaskic knew that these civilians were being used to dig trenches on the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, do I assume. As I said, I had contacts with his subordinates, and whether he knew, you would have to ask someone else that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you what your assumption was, operating in the Lasva Valley at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Relevance of the witness's assumption. If he has any knowledge, no objection fine, but relevance as to his assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What was that I got the from the interpreter, irrelevant? I don't know. I think that the question is a legitimate one. The witness has said that he worked for the HVO and for the commanders, so it is quite legitimate to ask what he assumes about the accused. The witness, I think, said that he didn't know. You can rephrase your question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is quite simple, Mr. Rajic. During this period of time did you assume that Blaskic knew that these civilians were being used to dig trenches in frontline areas?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: At that time I didn't really give it any thought. Now I can think about it and now I can make assumptions, but at that time I simply didn't think about it because, as I said, I was in contact with other persons and at other levels of command, so I really didn't think about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here now, what is your assumption?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, my assumption is probably that he might have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about these individual diggers on these work platoons. If I might just have one moment to discuss a point with my colleague before I move to the next point. Now, if I might just go -- ask one follow-up -- two follow-up questions to the issue that I just discussed with you concerning the selection of these people to dig trenches. You noted -- you just dealt with brigade commanders and not necessarily with Colonel Blaskic who put requests in for people to come dig trenches. During that period of time, did you get any requests from members of the HV, the Croatian army, to put work platoons together to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No, and I was not in any contact with the members of the Croatian army. No requests came in and, as I said, I did not have any contact with the members of the Croatian army in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying, Mr. Rajic, in the case of Prosecutor versus Aleksovski, and the date you testified was the 25th of August of 1998? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I remember the testimony. Perhaps I do not remember all the details, but if I were reminded, I could remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just read this back to you, and, counsel, it's on page 3.235 of that, and you were asked this question. "Q. Well, who was responsible overall for the function and collecting of the units for work duties? Was that you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
