utterances.text: What line, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The line we start is 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 3.235. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was -- I'll read that again, Mr. Rajic, in fairness, so we can put the entire matter in context. "Q. Well, who was responsible overall for the function and collecting of the units for work duties? Was that you?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Among others, I was one of them, but there were the commanders of the units if a situation required this." And I'm pausing so the interpreters can interpret this along. "Q. And the commanders of the units would be commanders of the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Members of the HVO, the commanders of the HVO, if it was their members. If it was the HV, then it would be those commanders."

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I never said that it was the Croatian army. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We'd ask for the tape. We'd ask that the tape be checked, the Registrar's Office check the tape, because the next question, Mr. President, is: "Q. And isn't it true that you were responsible for the HVO units?" There is no reaction, there is no follow-up to any comment about the HV. It seems very, very odd to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is very, very odd is the fact that this witness, in this testimony, is making a distinction between HVO commanders and HV commanders --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Or he's repeating --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I didn't interrupt you. The answer says: "A. Members of the HVO, the commanders of the HVO, if it was their members. If it was the HV, then it would be those commanders." There is a clear distinction, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, between two different military entities, the HVO and the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Or a repetition. We don't know. We will know from the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would ask the Registrar's Office to get the tape. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I propose, first of all, to keep calm, and I want to know whether you have a long way to go yet. Do you still have many questions, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a little bit, Judge. Not a long way to go. Probably I can finish by 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like us to speed up, please. That is the powers of the President, to require speeding-up of the process. Regarding the transcript, it is up to the parties, if they question what is in the transcript, to verify it. You will plead on this point later on. For the moment, it will suffice for us to ask the witness whether he recalls having said that. If he says he doesn't, we go on to your next question. In your closing statements, each of you will plead on the basis of that transcript if you consider it to be important. Did you also refer not only to the HVO but also to the HV? Do you remember saying that in the testimony you gave in the Aleksovski case, Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, we need your authorisation to get the tape from that case. It is in open session. If the Court grants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Quite. Why not? Of course, of course. It was a public hearing. We will clear up that point. If the witness can't answer or, rather, he cannot confirm that answer, we will postpone it for a later date. But I do wish us to speed up, please. Continue, Mr. Kehoe. In the meantime, the registrar, during the lunch break, can get the transcript for you to verify this. But let's not go back to that question. You will use it, both parties, in your closing statements. We cannot go back to things repeatedly during the hearing. This trial started in 1997 and we wish to finish it, so let's continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, with regard to the work units, were the Muslims segregated from others in these work units, i.e., were there Muslim work units and Romani work units and Croat work units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This was at the beginning of 1992, while we were still working together under the same roof and in the same offices because the Muslims reported to the officials of the department who were Muslims and the Croats reported to those who were in that department and who were Croats and -- I mean, I'm talking about Travnik. At that point in time, we coordinated these things. Later on, in Travnik, in that small part of Travnik that remained under HVO control, there weren't any Muslims who were engaged in work units and work platoons to dig trenches for the needs of the HVO, but in Travnik, there were Croats who were engaged to dig trenches for the needs of the HVO, and this was the larger part of the territory --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the BH army, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: And that was the larger part of the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, throughout the Lasva Valley area, were the work units segregated, i.e., were there Romanies in one unit, Muslims in another unit, and Croats in another unit, and when I say "throughout the Lasva Valley," I'm talking about in addition to the Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I do not know about that, but I think only the Romany were divided and that the rest were together -- were separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive information that Bosnian Muslims working on the frontlines in these work platoons had been killed?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I said that I do not know about any cases of any Muslims being killed, but I know of the case of an entire work platoon that was killed and it consisted of Croats primarily and perhaps there were two or three Serbs in that work platoon too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Bosnian Muslims that were wounded on these work platoons at the frontline; did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I don't know. If they were wounded, they were treated like everyone else in the hospital we had at Nova Bila. I assumed that it was that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that HVO soldiers were beating some of these individuals that were digging trenches on these work platoons?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you -- by the way, who was your counterpart in the National Defence Secretariat in Vitez after 1993 or during 1993? Would that have been Mario Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak was not. That I know. I think it was Stipo Zigonic who holds that post until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in these work units, were these work unit individuals considered to be part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, yes. In a certain sense, they were considered to be members of the HVO, and now, as these certificates were issued to all, regardless of ethnic background, this was -- this was recognised for all as their participation in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention to the indictment itself -- and this is my conclusory area of questioning, Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen -- in April, into the early part of May of 1993, Bosnian Muslims were incarcerated in, among other places, the Vitez cinema, the Dubravica school, Kaonik camp near Busovaca, the SDK offices in Vitez, and testimony has come to this Chamber that the Bosnian Muslim men in those locations were taken out to dig trenches on the frontline positions. Do you know about that, sir? Now, this is after Ahmici, which took place on the 16th of April, 1993. But do you know about these Bosnian Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What part of the indictment? Which count, Mr. Prosecutor? Which is the count?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am dealing with the paragraph 12, Mr. President, where those items are listed, those individual locales. It would be Counts 15 to 20. I believe they're repeated in another location as well, but that just happens to be the place that I'm reading from.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I do not know of such cases because we, in Travnik, had too many problems of our own because some Croats had been killed, there were certain incidents, and I was one of those who tried to calm the situation down so that there wouldn't be wider conflicts. Regrettably, what happened did happen, but as regards the specific cases that you're asking me about, I don't know of them because, as I said, every day, every day, we had incidents in Travnik, and that was a far more complex and bigger case than Vitez was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is you don't know anything about these Muslims being incarcerated in these locales; is that correct? You don't know anything about it at all?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: That's right. But I didn't have to know either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of conclusory questions, Mr. Rajic, and I will be through. And I will be through, Mr. President, before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You see, a bit of guidance achieves conciliation. You said that the cross-examination will be completed by 1.00, and I'm very glad that it will be before that, so please proceed with your last question and then, in the afternoon, Mr. Nobilo will have his right to re-examine and then perhaps the Judges will have some questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajic, what rank did you hold in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I received a rank in mid 1994. I was a sergeant (sic). Up till then, I did not have any rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your period of time, did you receive any awards from President Tudjman based on your service during the conflict in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I did not receive anything of that kind for participating in the fighting from anyone, any awards or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any awards at all from the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The rank was Major a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Neither from the Republic of Croatia nor from General Blaskic, so when I say "from nobody," this implies neither from the Republic of Croatia, no medals, no distinctions, or anything, awards for merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might just clear up one item in the record, Mr. President? I believe that initially the translation came across that he achieved the rank the sergeant in mid 1994, and I think the interpreters corrected it to say that he received the rank of Major. I think we all agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Rajic, do you carry a passport from the Republic of Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo doesn't have any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will re-ask the question. Do you carry and travel on a passport from the Republic of Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rajic. You've been very helpful. Thank you for coming. Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, counsel, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. It is ten to 1.00. Mr. Nobilo, do you have many questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I haven't got many, but I don't think I'll be able to complete them by 1.00. It's difficult to say. But I don't have many. I can try and start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, we're going to have a break which will allow us to restore calm to this testimony. Mr. Registrar, can you find the part of the tape that is in question so that we can achieve complete harmony between the Prosecution and the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And that is why we are giving you, Mr. Registrar, ten minutes extra time, so we will now adjourn and resume at 2.00 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing can resume now. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the witness brought in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a point of order before the witness does come in. The transcript itself, a tape, was reviewed by both Defence and Prosecution, and the transcript, the official transcript, in the Aleksovski case is incorrect. What reads in the transcript: "If it was the HV, then it would be those commanders." This transcript should read: "When it was in the army of BiH it was those commanders." Now, where the translation came between the HV and army BiH, none of us were there. Nonetheless, there was a discrepancy between this official transcript in the Registrar's office and the tape that I think everybody has listened to, and I think Defence counsel will agree with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, of course we agree. It was quite clear the "BH army," "Armija BiH." "BiH" is a local abbreviation for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. You're a good sport there I can see. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, you know, if you're right you're right, if you're wrong you're wrong. We went on the basis of the transcript. This is the official transcript. I do note that maybe for the Aleksovski transcript, the registrar might want to notify someone with regard to this transcript, that this transcript is, in fact, incorrect. I don't know if it is of any consequence in that trial. I don't know if it's of any consequence in that trial. I'm not aware of all facts in that trial, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy would like to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that goes back to what the Prosecutor said. Apparently both parties listened to the cassette in BCS. The transcripts, of course, are prepared from the interpretation and that is what is authoritative, unless something incorrect has been discovered, but the transcript in and of itself is not false because it's supposed to reproduce what was heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but there is still a problem because the transcript does not express what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Well, it happens rather frequently, in one of the -- either of the official languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Registrar, you will submit all of this discussion to the Presiding Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I won't fail to do so, Your Honour, and I also point out, in order for us to be complete, that the French version was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Almost everybody is right, starting with the French Judge who is satisfied by the fact that his language was correct. All right. That's the end of this incident, which means, my dear colleagues from both sides of the bench, that when you put forth arguments with such certitude that one is right, you always have to be careful, as all legal people must be. And having said these words of wisdom, I can have this witness brought in so that Mr. Nobilo can exercise his re-examination right. (The witness entered court) Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Rajic. Mr. Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I shall try to be brief in order to save as much time as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, tell me, to the best of your knowledge, when Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded from Yugoslavia, just like when Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia, these newly formed states, at the moment of gaining their independence, did they take over the laws of the former system of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know about Croatia but I do know about Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were mainly taken over, the regulations of the former Yugoslavia, because there wasn't enough time to pass new ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then tell me once again, and also tell us whether your colleagues from the Muslim part of the civilian authorities in Travnik applied these two bylaws that you spoke of today and which elaborate in detail the work obligation.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: These are the regulations that we did apply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the Muslim part of the civilian authorities in Travnik, did they also mobilise work platoons and send them to the frontlines towards anyone, the Serbs or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I know they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, did you ever see or ever hear that the Croatian army was in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I never saw or never heard of the Croatian army being in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I imagine, in view of your position, that you would have had to know had a unit from the Croatian army come to the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: All of us would have known for sure, but I know that no one did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it came, would that unit have made the people thrilled, all the people thrilled?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're waiting a bit for the purposes of translation. You said that in '98 the work platoons got the same status like the HVO, like the fighters, the soldiers. And tell me, in 1993, were they considered to be members of military units or were they considered to be members of a special organisation that were called work units?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No. They were not members of the military units. They were members of -- they were citizens who fulfilled their obligation through work obligation units, and in this way fulfilled their work obligation, and they were not those who had a military obligation. And later, or, rather, during the course of this year, work in work obligation units was made equal to that of the status of those who were entitled to receive certificates for participation in the war. All members of work obligation units, regardless of whether they were in the BH army or in the HVO received this status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you got a rank in 1994. Before that period, before 1994, was there an official system of ranks in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't any ranks. The commanders addressed each other in terms of the locations where they were. I don't know of anything else. So it was only after the Washington Accords that I got my rank too. It was sometime in April or May. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have dual citizenship, both of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. I'm first and foremost a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I also availed myself of the opportunity of having dual citizenship and that is the citizenship of the Republic of Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you about your passport. When did you have this passport issued?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Exactly on the 23rd of January, 1993, because I had to go to Switzerland. I had to travel, and I did not have any other travel documents. There weren't any. And I also had the old passport of the former Yugoslavia. However, at that time it was no longer possible to travel. I needed visas or something, whereas a Croatian passport allowed me to travel unimpeded in the countries of Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And today are new passports being issued of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or do you still have these problems?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: There are still some problems, because agreement has not been reached yet on the design of the passports. So I think that it is going to be the High Representative, Mr. Carlos Westendorp, who will have to rule on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more thing, I would like to draw your attention to one more thing. You said the work obligation, just like the military obligation, is a form of civic obligation of every citizen, vis-a-vis the defence of the country. So tell us, if we were to define those who are fulfilling their military obligations while serving in the army, and the members of work platoons and all other citizens who were not involved in terms of military obligation or work obligation, so -- I'm talking about children, I'm talking about old people over 65, and pregnant women. So if we look at these criteria, how could we divide the population? I hope you've understood what I've been trying to say.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, I have understood you. In my opinion, pure civilians were those who did not have any one of the assignments that I mentioned in terms of those five obligations, and those were men over 65 and younger than 16, and women over 55 and pregnant women. And there's one more category. So these were the persons who could not be mobilised according to the law, and who were not mobilised therefore. And there was another category of people who could not have been mobilised, and those are persons who were not capable of fulfilling this obligation, which they were duty bound to carry out according to the law and constitution. And then there was a military medical commission that had to proclaim such persons either capable of or incapable of fulfilling a certain obligation of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is one group of citizens that you defined who did not have to carry out a military duty or a work duty, and if we look at it that way, how would we define the members of the work units? Are they soldiers, are they equal to the civilians who did not have any obligations whatsoever, or are they a third category?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: This would have to be a third category, because they are not soldiers. Soldiers are the ones who fight with weapons in their hands. But there are those who did not have any obligations whatsoever either. So it is a category of citizens that in case of war or immediate threat of war does have certain tasks which are not of purely military nature but do serve the purpose, so to speak, of these armed formations and not only their purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at all of this now, retirement insurance, years of service, shares that were issued and salaries, et cetera that a soldier is entitled to and that a person who had a work obligation has, is a civilian who did not have any such obligations, does he have any one of these entitlements, either on the side of the HVO or the BH army?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No, no. This kind of civilian does not have any such entitlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also let's put another hypothetical question, as my learned colleague had put. A Muslim in Vitez digs trenches for a year, for example. Does he have the same rights like a member of the Croat people who was in the HVO? Today does he have the same entitlement?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: As far as I know, all have equal entitlements, all of them who participated in certain units, of work obligation units or military units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, in conclusion, am I right when I say that it is my understanding that there are three groups. One, pure civilians, total civilians, and these other two --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. We've been through this just now. This has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Nobilo was not asking exactly the same question. I think there is a difference, Mr. Kehoe. Continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is my last question: Did I understand you correctly, and perhaps this can be a touchstone for all the participants in this trial, can we say, in view of one's involvement in the war, there are three groups of persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have thus concluded the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Let me turn to my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Actually, witness, I don't want to ask you any questions, I only want to compliment you on insisting that the record in Aleksovski was not correct, and in congratulating counsel on both sides for reaching agreement as to what the position really was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Yes, that's how we must proceed when one is in a legal institution. I have one or two questions that I'd like to ask you Mr. Rajic. I thought that the text of 1989 relating to National Defence had been conceived at a time when people thought that the danger might come from a country other than the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Here is my question: Don't you have the feeling that by -- when using those texts, that is the one of 1989 or the one that was reworked by the Croatian defence community, don't you have the impression that they were somewhat distorted from their original meaning, insofar as -- insofar as it is conceivable that one can organise civilian defence and military defence when you think that the homeland is in danger, the homeland being the six republics, in a way, isn't it distorting power the same way to use the same framework, the same organisation, but to use it against a brother people under the pretext that one is temporarily enemies? You who have studied political science, isn't that kind of a distortion of powers?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there has been any actual distortion, because they were regulations which were applicable under such conditions as well, and there weren't any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I notice that in 1989 people thought that the Croats would fight against the Chetniks or the Muslims. Is that what that meant?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: No. We did not know who would be fighting whom. At least I didn't know, and I don't think the people knew, most of the people knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was sure that nobody knew. Nobody had foreseen those events. Nonetheless, it remains true that when in the text one says that the work platoons were going to build fortifications, I think that in the mind of Marshal Tito and his successors, that meant, like in other countries, I come from a country which was invaded on many occasions, that all resources have to be used for work, each person in his own place. There needed to be people who worked in communications, there needed to be soldiers, there needed to be generals, there needed to be people who worked in artillery, there needed to be statisticians, and then people who dig trenches. Therefore, my second question is to ask you whether you yourself dug trenches. Did you go to dig trenches yourself?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I did not dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you are telling us that the -- that the system that was used for those people who were digging trenches was a proper one?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are telling us that the work system that governed the work that had to be done, that is digging the trenches, this was a proper, this was a suitable type of system?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Well, that is a point that can be discussed. That is to say, what in a war, a war that nobody expected, and particularly not expected it to be the kind of war it was, it is difficult, as I say. We had to makeshift and make do, and adjust ourselves to the situation in hand, because -- and you yourself noted very aptly we were preparing for an external enemy of some kind, where all of us together would use all our strength and force to resist that enemy, but this unfortunate war that took place in our country was a little different than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's what I'm saying, that texts were used that had been designed for aggression coming from the outside, but they were used for what could be called an internal war. I suppose (sic) there is no other component. My final question is to know whether these work units that went to dig trenches, were they sent to the frontlines against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: The work platoons which were under my command were not sent there. The Muslims were not sent to the frontlines towards the Muslims. These were only the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But trenches were used on the frontline against the Bosnian army. That's what it was done for.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, those trenches were used for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In the document that was provided to us, the decree on the organisation of Herceg-Bosna is, of course, a decree which went back to the decrees of 1989. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps you don't know -- since you are a member of the HVO, I guess you should know, you have Croatian nationality, the decision which established the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna you are familiar with, I assume. That was in November of 1991. You know that, since you like the idea of belonging to that community and you know when it was established, that is, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, I know when it was created, when the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was created, and whether it's an idea I liked, I don't know, but that was the reality of the times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That isn't my question. That's a reality which became concrete. It was a decision that was taken by Mr. Mate Boban on the 19th of November, 1991. My question is to know whether that Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was established to fight against the Muslims in the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not. It was created to protect, first and foremost, the Croatian people from the then aggression of the JNA and the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am pleased that you agree with me about that because the presentation of the reasons for the decision state that by organising a Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, it was a way of fighting against the Chetnik aggression. Therefore, I would be right to believe that the trenches that people had to dig on the front in the struggle against the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were trenches that were not legal.

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: Whether they were legal or not, it is up to you to assess and judge, but the fact remains that there was a conflict and that the trenches served the function of defence in a certain area for the defence of the Croatian people in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, you agree with me when I say that in the end, not only the decree which is covered by the 14th of November, 1994 -- 494 that had been set up in order to organise in the case of a conflict coming from the outside, of aggression on the outside against the republic, but in addition, that the decree of 1992, the one of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, also distorted your own organisation which means a defence organisation which was supposed to be used against the Chetniks. Would you be in agreement with what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: In part, I do agree, yes, but at that time, there was the disintegration and non-functioning of the State organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we were conscious of the fact that the war which broke out in Croatia would not end in Croatia but would be expanded; and Herceg-Bosna, quite simply, was an instrument of organisation for the Croatian people to stand up to that, and the fact is that later on there was a conflict with the BH army. But everything that was done to fortify the lines, towards the one side first and then the other side, we, in Bosnia, at one point were fighting -- everybody was fighting everybody else and everybody did what they could in a situation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps at that point the ones who were the weakest were not able to fight in the same way because, pursuant to these texts, when a general mobilisation effort was being made, that is the invasion of a country, when a country is invaded, all of the forces have to be called in to defend the country, but here you are running the risk that one of the parties would not go to the trenches in very good spirits, even though yesterday there was a witness who appeared to be satisfied about having gone to the trenches. But that's another problem. All right. I think we can't say anything further, but I can conclude by saying that basically, when, during your testimony, you tell us that the texts for you were an obligation for all citizens, would you be agreeable with me when I say that a certain category of citizens perhaps was not quite in agreement with the objectives that you were pursuing?

utterances.speaker: Tomislav Rajic
utterances.text: They did not perhaps agree with the objectives, some citizens, that is, but all citizens who were capable of performing certain functions were duty-bound - although they had the right as well - but they were duty-bound to participate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In any case, you have carried out what you were asked to do here at the Tribunal, and the Tribunal thanks you for having done so. You have spoken about that part of the indictment which we needed clarifications for. Thank you very much. You have completed your testimony. We are going to have you accompanied out of the courtroom, and then we can move to the testimony of the following witness who should, I believe, be the last one. Thank you once again, Mr. Rajic. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the last witness for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fourmy, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: I apologise for intervening again, but this is for the transcript, the English transcript, from what I can read on the Live Note system. On page 402 (sic), lines 12 and 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How can you find the lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Because I noted them down. But I think that the Defence and the Prosecutor and myself, the registrar, we have a way of going up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Not the Judges, though. We can't go up on the screen? We can't scroll up?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: The Judges have all powers except for the one of going backwards into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You see, we thought we had all the powers, but we can't do this. What do you want to say to us, Mr. Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: On page 82, lines 12 and 13, instead of "I suppose there is no other competent" -- instead of -- it should say "assuming there is no other competent." And on page 84 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Defence may be able to scroll backwards into the transcript, but we've never done it and we don't know how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: And on page 84 on line 20, you referred, in one of your questions that you asked the witness, to Exhibit D494.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: And what came up was 14 November. The date was given instead of the number. And then the court reporter said that they would have to check that. So it should be 494. I can help them. It was D494. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You see, everyone really stands in admiration for your vigilance, and once again I would like to thank you for being at the hearings and displaying such competence. All right. Mr. Nobilo, if you could go on, please? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, sir? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the Judges, please give us your name, your first name, the date and place of your birth, your profession, and your current residence, since this is a public hearing, and after that, we will ask you to remain standing to take the oath and then you can sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ivo Mlivoncic. I was born in Vares, near Sarajevo, in 1931. I have been living in Split for 40 years. I am a citizen of the Republic of Croatia. I am a journalist by profession. I live and work in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated now. Thank you for having come to the International Criminal Tribunal where, for some time now, there has been a trial being conducted in this Tribunal of Mr. Tihomir Blaskic who is in the courtroom to your left. You will first be asked some questions by the Defence, then by the Prosecutor. Mr. Nobilo, please have the name of the witness given again because I wasn't able to catch it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Mlivoncic, would you, by way of introduction, tell us something about your life and work? You were born in 1931 in Vares, which is Central Bosnia and the region that we have been dealing with for several years here now. So briefly describe your life and work and your qualifications.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Well, here it is. I was born in a working family, worker's family, in Vares. I went to a four-year elementary school at the classical gymnasium in Visoko, the Franciscan classical gymnasium in Visoko. After that I studied theology in Sarajevo and graded in Ljubljana from the faculty of theology there. After that, I graduated the history of archeology at the faculty of philosophy in Zadar and also graduated at the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade. As a journalist for Slobodna Dalmacija in Split, I have been working since 1940-something, I dealt with history, sociological research, religion, religious communities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're being signalled to by our interpreters who ask you to slow down, please, and please make pauses because all this is being translated into two languages, and it is in the interests of the Defence and the Court and the Prosecutors for us to hear what you are saying properly.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: As a journalist, I dealt with scientific work and history, sociological studies and politicalogical studies and research, religion -- of religions and religious communities as well, and that is how I became a journalist specialising in religious matters, particularly relationships between religion and politics, the Church and the State, and I have written many articles and comments, particularly with regard to Catholicism, Orthodoxy, and Islam, and I have had a series of interviews with theological scientists, Catholic, Orthodox, Islamic, and with people from the hierarchy of the religious communities such as bishops, archbishops, muftis, and so on and so forth, therefore -- and I have written two books on the subject, one book is entitled "The Church in Latin America," that is a book on the theology of liberation. My second book is "The Pope and the Croats," the State and cultural ties between the papacy and the Croatian people. And my third book, the latest book that I wrote, it is "Crimes with a Stamp," and it was a book that came out one month ago, and it has a subtitle, "The Crimes of Genocide, War Crimes, the Muslim Bosniak forces against Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina." I wrote a lot about this subject matter in the Balkanika, an Italian journal, three years ago. This was my first research, whereas now I have published my comprehensive research. So I have written about this subject matter a great deal in the different newspapers that I worked for and in my own matrix newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Mlivoncic, and once again, let us make some breaks between our sentences, we are drawing closer to the subject that you have been called here to testify about. You have written a book which represents a review of crimes by Muslims over the Croats in this last war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what your motives for this were, why you entered into this specific type of subject matter at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: When, in Stupni Do, the war crime was committed, it was a village in the municipality in which I was born, about three kilometres from the house in which I was born. The first individual who described this crime was me publicly, and I informed the Cardinal Franjo Puharic about this, the archbishop, and the President of the Mesihat of the Muslim community for Bosnia and Croatia and Slovenia, Mr. Zevko Efendja Omerpasic. That was a moral act on my part, and I reacted to this phenomenon and I learnt about the facts of that particular case. But as the public kept -- there was -- repetition was made that there were crimes committed about the Bosniaks in Ahmici and Stupni Do, this has been repeated again and again, this motivated me to state publicly and to caution the people of the crimes that had actually taken place and had been perpetrated by the Muslim Bosniak forces over the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was my motive for showing that it was not only the extremists in my own Croatian people who had committed some crimes but that crimes were committed by extremists in the Muslim Bosniak -- amongst the Muslim Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, before we move on to concrete matters, your research, tell us which methods you used to collect data? Would you explain that to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I'm a journalist by profession, and so I had my basic five W's: who, what, where, when, and why, and I tried to answer those basic journalistic questions. In order to supply answers to those questions, I developed my own methodology, and I myself deal in scientific research work and, of course, I used my own documentation as a journalist, I travelled around the country to visit the places where the crimes had taken place and where the fighting went on between the HVO and BH army, and I covered a lot of ground. I had occasion to see a grenade exploding in Mostar. I was in Sarajevo when the Pope was to go there on a visit in 1994 and he wasn't able to come because there was shelling and a shell hit one of the houses near where I was staying. And in Stolac, I was arrested by the -- I was detained, I was not arrested, I was detained by the Croatian police to see what I was doing there, and in my native town of Vares, the Muslim Bosniak police detained me and asked me to hand over my camera and everything else. I did not allow this. I also felt a Chetnik Kalashnikov on my own back in Knin. So these are all moments and instances which show that I actually moved around the terrain, and I also had the possibility of gaining an insight into the documentation of the commission to ascertain the crimes of the Croatian community -- given me by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. These are a lot of documents, comprising 10.000 different documents, which are relevant for this subject matter, and I looked through and read through all these documents. I had them all in my hands. Next, I collected documentation from the religious communities themselves, from the Catholic Church, from the Sarajevo and Bosnian bishopcy (sic), from the Mostar bishopcy, and from the Bosnia-Herzegovinan provinces coming under the Franciscans, and I can say that these documents which I asked for and sought in the religious communities, that there aren't many of them. According to the rules, every parish priest had to record what had happened on a day-by-day report for his parish, a chronicle of the parish done by the parish priest. However, most of these facts and figures were lacking, and when I asked Father Janko Rubos, who was the parish priest in Bugojno during the war and he is now in Fojnica, why he did not keep records of this, he told me he was afraid and that if the Muslim Bosniak authorities come and see me, keeping a record of this, I might have fared the worst for it. So that there was no possibility for having a testimony of what was going on. But I should also like to mention that many documents were not accessible to me. I was not able to go to certain places. For example, I was only able to visit Grbavica near Mostar very recently. I could not even think about going to Orasac. This is a village between Travnik and Zenica, and it was impossible for me to go there, because in a Catholic village there, the Mujahedins came and they forbid anybody return to that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please slow down a bit and try to make a small pause when you describe all the methods that you used.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I used authentic sources, and we can also say that I found other documents in what was published in the daily press and in weeklies, so there are quite a few documents in that respect too, but these documents are not always reliable because they were often under the influence of different interests, what should be published or what should not be published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You completed this research of yours in June 1997 and you prepared a manuscript which is based on your research, and tell me, have you stopped since then or have you continued your investigations?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: No, I did not stop, and as I wrote in the forward to my book that my book is not final, that perhaps there are some inaccuracies in it too, something that has not been sufficiently clarified or explained, perhaps I did not have counter-documents, so I continued to investigate, and I can mention a few things to you. In my research, I tried to touch upon the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President and counsel. I would object to the witness -- he appears to be reading from a prepared text, and if he needs notes to refresh his recollection, I would ask him to use those notes, but to -- I have watched him for the past few minutes. He appears to be reading and then turning the page and going to the next page and reading that page, so I object to this form of answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know that in legal institutions, at least in this one, the witness has to testify freely. The witness can bring documents that have been worked on. He may have documents, but only for statistics or to refresh his memory. That's natural. And he can do that with the authorisation of the opposing party. Therefore, I must ask you, excuse me, if you are reading a pre-prepared document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It seems to me that the witness did not get any interpretation. Perhaps the channel has been changed. Could you please check that for us? Mr. President, this statement is going to involve a lot of numbers, a lot of figures, a lot of dates, and you can't really speak about this off the cuff, you have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't think that that's what Mr. Harmon's objection was. The objection that I sustained and support -- first of all, do you hear me, sir? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The objection of the opposing parties is the following: You cannot read a pre-prepared document. You can use personal notes with the authorisation of the Trial Chamber, but you cannot come in and then take a document from your briefcase which you begin to read. That you cannot do. You must answer the questions according to your memory. When you need a date or a specific statistic, you can look at the statistics on documents on the ELMO, for example, you can give that to the opposing party, but you cannot read a document. All right. Make an effort, please. I'm sure that you will be able to do so. However, if your memory fails you and you need to consult your notes, I will authorise you to do so. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, and I apologise. Perhaps you have the wrong impression. I wasn't reading at all. I just kept glancing at the places that I had highlighted. I wasn't reading. Perhaps it looks as if I were reading, but I'm not reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Just try not to read the document. I'm sure you're very familiar with it. You're a historian, a journalist, a researcher; you should be able to speak almost without any documents, I'm sure of that. If you need to do so with our authorisation, you can refer to your notes. Perhaps we could go back to the questioning, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was, and you said "Yes," that you continued your research after 1997, after you finished most of your research and when you started preparing the manuscript of your last book. So tell me, in this additional research of yours, and nothing has been written about it as yet in your book, did you reach some information which could be of interest for this trial?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Naturally, I continued with my research, aware of the fact that even what I had collected until now was a minimum and that there will certainly be even more information about all the victims, so I continued my research, and after I handed in my manuscript in June 1997, in July I went to Kiseljak and I got in touch with the mother of General Blaskic, his sister, et cetera, and I got a new piece of information this way that I was unaware of; and I didn't know that General Blaskic's father, Ivo Blaskic, who was born in 1933, was in the HVO, in the medical corps, and I think that on the 12th of November, 1993, he was killed at the point in time when he had a Red Cross band on his arm and when he was carrying drugs for the wounded, and this will be published in the second edition of my book, and he will be included as one of the victims of this war. Then also a few words about the name of General Blaskic. In the documents, we have seen Teofil and things like that, and that name doesn't exist. In the parish where General Blaskic was baptised, it says that his name is Teofil. "Teos" is "God," "fil" is "to love," and we translate that into Croat as "Bogoljub," but amongst the immediate members of his family, he was always called Tihomir. About his family, about his roots, and about how he was brought up, his parish priest spoke of this and spoke of him very nicely, and I published this in one of my articles in "Nedeljna Dalmacija," weekly paper, and then I asked some other people what they thought about him as a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please answer the questions the Defence is asking you. If you're asked a question about the honourable origins about the accused's family, you can answer, but we don't have a great deal of time. You are here to speak inter alia about the substance of your book. Mr. Nobilo try to focus your witness's testimony on what you think essential for the Defence of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mlivoncic, now we are going to distribute a set of maps that will be a basis for your presentation. I would like to have these maps distributed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 495.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please put page 1 on the ELMO. Mr. Mlivoncic, could you tell us what this map depicts? First let us look at Bosnia and Herzegovina and the numbers that are in yellow areas. Could you tell the Court what this represents?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: This is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The green -- oh, it's yellow. Oh, all right. All right. It's yellow. So the areas marked in yellow are the areas of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina where a conflict broke out between the BH army and the HVO, and where Croats were victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the left-hand side is a survey. Certain numbers -- the total number of victims, could you comment on that a bit?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: These figures show the following: That the total number of war victims, Croats, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to my research, was 1.606.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. When you say victims of the war, are you referring to victims in terms of persons killed in fighting, or persons who were killed as a result of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about civilians and prisoners of the HVO who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: So one can see here that out of that number, there are 968 adult civilians, 120 children, and 518 imprisoned soldiers of the HVO. I said that number of 1.606 victims is a minimal number, because I'm sure that later research will show, and I have already shown this, that this figure is even bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the total number of Croat refugees from the municipalities marked in yellow on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: According to my investigations, during the conflict between the BH army and the HVO, expellees and the refugees among the Croat people number around 140.000. And if we compare this to the figures concerning expelled Bosniak Muslims at the same time, from the same area, there were 50.000 of them. Speaking in terms of percentage, and compared to the census from 1991, that was, out of the total number of Croats, 19.5 per cent turn out to be refugees and expellees, and Bosniak Muslims 2.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of that is in the area marked in yellow where there was a conflict between the Croatian and Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it is also at the time of the conflict, not before and not after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these figures do not include at all fighting with the Chetniks on either side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: May I just add one more interesting figure? Of 120 children --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer your question -- answer the question and then we're going to correct the record, the transcript. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: This is a very interesting figure, for one reason, because Alija Izetbegovic, at a rally commemorating the fifth anniversary of the BH army, said in public that the BH army did not kill children, and old men, and women and children. So those words of his are in deep contradiction to my research.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript did not include my question -- rather, your answer. These victims, these refugees are only the result of the Croat Muslim conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Only from the conflict between the BH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let us move quickly, and in terms of facts, because all of this is going to be tendered into evidence later, on the next page, number 1 is the town of Rama Prozor. Could you please tell us, according to your research, in the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, what is the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- here on the map it says that the total number of victims was 66 in the municipality of Rama Prozor. Out of that figure 34 were HVO prisoners of war, 26 adult civilians, and 6 children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And refugees, 3.500; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us move on to the next document. Could you please explain to the Court what this map represents?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: This map represents locations where terrible things were done to the Croat people in the village of Jurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What municipality was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Rama Prozor. And then in the municipality of Uzdol where there were 41 victims, and the municipality of Hudutsko with 22 victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the dates when the crimes were committed can be seen on the white spaces, together with the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to the next map.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: The next map shows the area of the municipality of Jablanica, in which there was a total number of 69 Croat victims, out of them 11 adults --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you're going to take each of the maps, you know, the Judges have the maps. Perhaps you could ask questions about specific points that are not clear. But it's clear that the Judge -- that the witness is giving the Judges and the Prosecution municipalities -- maps of municipalities. He's done civilian censuses, refugees, HVO civilians of Croatian nationality. Perhaps you might ask questions that would add to the information that's on the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can apply different methods. It is true that these maps are rather self-explanatory and clear, so perhaps in order to save time, of course the Trial Chamber is going to look at all these maps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In the cross-examination the Prosecution -- if the Prosecution, in the cross-examination, is going to use one of the cards that the witness has given, then you can go back to the map in question during the redirect, but as regards the way you're asking the questions, I think that the Judges are satisfied with what's -- what shows up on all of these detailed maps, unless you want to add something either regarding the method or this or that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I agree that we should save time. These maps are very well presented, and they do provide the right kind of information concerning figures. So perhaps in addition to what you have already said, we could look at some of the conclusions that you drew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mlivoncic, in order to save time, we are not going to go through each and every one of these municipalities, because these maps are evidence in their own right, and when you finish we are going to tender them into evidence in this court. So let us move on to some typical forms of crimes that appeared to be new, on the basis of your research, and what are some of the conclusions that you drew from your research? So we are not going to go through each and every one of the municipalities where these crimes were committed, because I agree with the Judges, these maps which you made and for which you provided information are quite self-explanatory and clearly show the time and the place of the crimes committed. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I agree. During my research, I tried to link this up with the history of crime in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Every country has a history of crime, and so does Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as far as Bosnia is concerned, the Nobel prize winner Ivo Andric depicted this the best in his works. And let us look at the forms of killing and the ways in which persons were killed during the conflict between the BH army and the HVO. There is a new form of crime that can be observed, which was unknown until then in the history of crime in Bosnia. I call this ritual killing. Perhaps I should explain this to you better by giving certain examples. In the municipality of Travnik, in the village of Miletici, on the 24th of April, 1993, the Muslim Bosniak forces imprisoned 30 young persons, some of whom were civilians and some -- and others were HVO soldiers. They were lined up, or, rather, made to stand in a circle, and then they cut off the head of the first one on the left-hand side, they put it on a tray, and they gave it to each and every one of the others to kiss it, and then the other one's turn came and then the other, et cetera. And this was confirmed by witnesses. And it was also confirmed by the exhumation of these victims in 1996, which was carried out by the commission of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the assistance of the International Community, when bodies without heads were discovered. At the cemetery in Kandija (phoen) near Bugojno, the grave of an old man, Ilija Mostarac, was discovered, and a stick was stuck into his chest, another one into his neck and another one into his left-hand side. And this is a form of killing that is quite well known in a phenomenon which is called Dance Macabre. At the entrance to Bugojno, going from Kupres, at a military checkpoint manned by the BH army, the Mujahedin imprisoned three HVO soldiers. They then killed them and knelt down into his blood and thanked Allah for a job well done. Those are just some examples which show that crime in Bosnia-Herzegovina in this conflict, which is for me an unfortunate one and an unhappy one between the Croats and Muslims in -- and Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These new forms of killing were brought by the Mujahedin from the Islamic countries, and for the most part they took part in them. So that is one of my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mlivoncic. Mr. President, all these maps with all the facts and figures that they contain we are tendering as one piece of evidence. It's not necessary for us to assign numbers to each map. So this is evidence which I wish -- these are the documents which I wish to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you completed your direct-examination, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we will take a break, and then we can resume in 20 minutes for the cross-examination. We will suspend the hearing until quarter after four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, about how much time are you going to need? I'm keeping you under surveillance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would imagine, Mr. President, no more than a half an hour. It depends on the answers given to me by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's fine. Mr. Harmon, proceed, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mlivoncic, I believe if I have pronounced your name correctly. My name is Mark Harmon and my colleagues from the Prosecution bench include Mr. Gregory Kehoe, to my immediate right, and to his right Mr. Andrew Cayley. Let me first of all begin by asking you, please, to turn to the map on the Kiseljak municipality in Defence Exhibit 495. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please. I'm asking, please, Mr. Usher, this particular map. Thank you. Now, Mr. Mlivoncic, let me ask you, on the 18th of April, 1993, which side was responsible for the commencement of combat activities in the Kiseljak municipality on the 18th of April, 1994 (sic), the HVO or the Armija? What did your research show?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, on 18th April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I consider this question to be outside the frameworks of the examination-in-chief. Mr. Mlivoncic was called here to speak to us of the victims and not responsibility for the conflict and who attacked first or who is responsible for the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second, please, Mr. Mlivoncic. You have to wait until the Judges finish their consultation after Mr. Nobilo made his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to allow Mr. Harmon to ask the question. We don't know whether Mr. Harmon is going back to the problem of victims. I've already told you, Mr. Nobilo, and this is a guarantee for the Defence, that if on any specific map or any specific point the Prosecution develops a point, you, of course, in your redirect, can go back to that point and ask any questions you like. What is the purpose of your asking that question, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Because, Mr. President, as you will see, on the map there is a reference to the 18th of April, 1993 in Kiseljak, identifying seven victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question to Mr. Mlivoncic is: Who started the conflict on the 18th of April in Kiseljak? What did your research show?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness is in a position to answer, but you are a journalist, you, Mr. Mlivoncic. Would you please answer if you can?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer the question very happily. I did not research into who began first and who in a given situation began the conflicts. I did not study who is to blame for the conflicts. I studied the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that's the answer that the witness has given you. He's been called in to speak only about the victims. He has done some research on the Croatian victims. Would you please move to another question, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Gladly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference to the seven victims identified in Kiseljak on the 18th of April, 1993, who were those victims, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: The victims, I can't enumerate them now but I have them in my book by name and surname, and perhaps their date of birth as well. You have that in my book. I can't tell you off the bat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't have a copy of your book, it hasn't been published outside of the former Yugoslavia, as far as I know. Would you kindly refer to your book and identify the seven victims who perished on the 18th of April, 1993 in the city of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Just a moment please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will the Judges have the opportunity to have that work at the end of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would dare give it to the translation unit after all the materials we have given to them to translate. If you would like it you can make it your exhibit, but we have not submitted it to the translation unit because it is lengthy and voluminous, and it would be a great deal of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, we're not going to ask you to work under urgent conditions, but at the end of the proceedings, or the end of this trial, the Judges would like to have a translation of that work. Does that seem possible to you or are we going to have to pay royalties in order to do so, to re-copy it that is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: First of all, the document has to be submitted officially to the Trial Chamber. It has to be recognised as an exhibit. And further to your request, we could ask for a translation of relevant passages at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. If you agree, if you want it as an exhibit, we will work in that way, Mr. Nobilo, and you will indicate the relevant passages so we can have them translated. All right, continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that respect I would also ask that a copy of this book be made available to the Office of the Prosecutor so we also might indicate relevant passages, or at least read passages that this witness has based his testimony on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do not have a problem with that, other than a matter of principle. There were works of witnesses who testified for the Office of the Prosecutor that we cannot obtain. Dissertations and other things that just aren't available or were available somewhere where we could get them. I don't think we have a problem with the book but that was not the principle that was applied to the Defence during the Prosecution case, and so I think if Mr. Harmon has an informal request to the Defence, we might well entertain it, but in terms of a motion that has a legal basis, we reject the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps to counsel's unwillingness to give us a copy of this freely, if he would identify the publisher we would be glad to go out and buy a copy at our expense, but we need to know the publisher and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I think that we can settle that question quickly. The Defence will have the work tendered as an exhibit, that is. We ask the Defence to submit that as an exhibit and it will be given an exhibit number. In addition, the Judges ask that it be given to the Judges with the Defence number and with a copy sent to the Prosecution, so that if in the deliberations the Judges need it, each of the parties should know that this is a book which was part of the inter parte proceedings. You will give it now to the -- give it to the registrar but also tell us the publisher of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In order to comply with what you've just said, Mr. President, this will be 496, 496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can now go back to your testimony, and in that we can find -- did you find the names of the victims that you were asked to find by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I have looked inside, and I see that it is a document signed by the competent authorities of the HVO, without name and surname. Later on in my research I -- this is not in the book, but I haven't got the document with me. So I cannot comply with that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mlivoncic, did you then verify the deaths of those seven individuals? You don't have the document. Did you verify, either through victim testimony or witness testimony about the deaths of those particular seven people before you included it in your book?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Every document that I relied on I endeavoured to verify it. I had documents which were opposite in what they stated, opposite to each other, contrary in content. Then I would go in the field to talk to the families and relations of those individuals, and after that I listed the names and surnames. And the document that was put out by the HVO authorities with a signature and stamp, that was a proper document for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, but the HVO document, as I understood your testimony, didn't identify the seven victims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: When I collected material for my book I did not have an identification of the victims with their names and surnames, but later on, and this will be included in the second edition of my book, you will have the victim Ivan Blaskic. He too was a victim of war, and he is not included in the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Do you have and did you ever ascertain the names of the seven victims who were killed on the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have said a moment ago I have the document now in my archives, but I was not able to include it in my book because I got the document in the course of last year, last autumn, and I gave my manuscript for publication in 1997, in June. So this is a document that will be included in the second edition of my book when it comes out in print.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlivoncic, were the seven victims HVO soldiers who were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ages of those particular victims?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I can't remember them all, because there were 1.600 names and I can't remember those particular seven. It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you talk to the relatives of those particular seven victims, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I talked to Father Ivan Pervan the parish priest of Kiseljak, and he will do what is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it the answer to my question is you did not talk to the relatives of the seven alleged victims who perished in Kiseljak on 18th April, 1993, instead you talked to Father Pervan.

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: It's the parish priest, and he records into the book of deaths all the deaths of all his parishioners. They are his parishioners and so it is his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does Father Pervan record in the book of parishioners the facts and circumstances under which his parishioners died?

utterances.speaker: IVO MLIVONCIC
utterances.text: I have said, in explaining the methodology of my research, that I tried to find documents with the church authorities. The church authorities did not fulfil their canonic duties, that is to say, to keep records and chronicles of the parish that they should have done. There were rare examples.
